And it was maybe the only moment in OpenAI's history where I felt like I didn't want to do it anymore. / I think I've been very much approaching OpenAI through a lens of uncertainty, of feeling like I don't know what the right answer is. / And I think that a lot of what I've tried to do is have a stronger sense of self and a stronger sense of when there is conviction that we need to act on it. / we just waited too long. / I also really care about the environment in which these things are done. claims.claim: Greg Brockman was born in 1987 and grew up in Thompson, North Dakota, the son of two physicians, Drs. Ron Brockman and Ellen Feldman of Altru Health System. Forbes listed him as 38 in September 2026.
claims.inference: Stable biographical frame. Use the birth year; the full date (November 29) appears only in Wikipedia’s uncited infobox.
claims.alternative: Parents’ professions are from a 2007 local item and may have changed; describe them as of 2007 or omit.

claims.claim: He grew up on what he insists is a "hobby farm," not a farm, describing a "focused, quiet childhood" in which he milked cows, gathered eggs and fell in love with math studying on his own; OpenAI asked MIT Technology Review to correct the wording, and Hao noted that "Brockman considers this distinction important."
claims.inference: The correction request is a small, verified instance of attention to precise self-presentation.
claims.alternative: It may simply be accuracy (his parents were physicians, not farmers). Do not overread one correction; use it as a texture detail, not proof.

claims.claim: As a teenager he completed every math course at Red River High School, took classes at the University of North Dakota, won a silver medal at the 2006 International Chemistry Olympiad, attended Canada/USA Mathcamp, and in 2007 became the first North Dakota finalist in the Intel Science Talent Search since 1973.
claims.inference: Early, repeated competitive excellence across fields.
claims.alternative: Achievement alone is common to gifted teenagers of every type; it is not evidence of a Type 3 motive by itself.

claims.claim: Brockman says he planned to be an actor through ninth grade, had been the male lead in a play or two, and chose hard sciences over the arts because he wanted to "double down on something" where "I felt like I could be best in the world and really try to move the needle," judging it the area "where I could most make a difference."
claims.inference: He frames his formative life choice in terms of where he could be best and have the most impact, and he has a performer’s history. Supports an achievement/image reading of how he chose a path.
claims.alternative: A 2026 retrospective told on a podcast; "make a difference" also fits a mission-driven 1 or a 2. He also says he loved acting for "the group aspect of it."

claims.claim: His first paid job, at about 14, came from standing at attention "in character" while older applicants chatted during an extras audition for a Mannheim Steamroller concert; he was not picked, but the organizers said they loved "how much you were dedicated" and created a gingerbread-man role for him. He draws the lesson of "not always defaulting into the role, but trying to find creative ways to get it."
claims.inference: An early story of visible dedication that gets noticed and rewarded with a role made for him; he tells it as formative.
claims.alternative: Possibly polished in retelling and chosen for an entertaining interview; one anecdote, unverified by others.

claims.claim: He says North Dakota let him "really excel and be the best in the state at different areas that I put my mind to," chart his own course and "march to my own tune," where a high-powered school would have kept him on the standard track.
claims.inference: Self-understanding organized around standing out and being best.
claims.alternative: Also reads as a plain account of a gifted kid in a small state; no motive is proven.

claims.claim: After high school he took a gap year to write a chemistry textbook; told he could not publish without a PhD, he learned to code to put it online, and he describes his first game reaching 1,500 users in a day as "the most glorious feeling" and "This is what I want, I want to help people, I want to benefit people and build for them." He told Lex Fridman in 2019 that "a lot of what really motivates me is is building things" and prized the leverage by which "a single individual with an idea is able to affect the entire planet."
claims.inference: Building is tied, from the start, to others using and registering the work (users, hits, reach). Consistent across 2015, 2019 and 2026 tellings.
claims.alternative: Equally consistent with a service motive (Type 2) or simple builder satisfaction; the "help people" language is genuine-sounding and recurrent.

claims.claim: He left Harvard for MIT because, running the computer club as a sophomore, he felt "I’m not ready. I have so much to learn. I need to be around people who are so much better than me"; in 2016 he wrote he was "trying to constantly surround myself by people who I could learn from and build something useful with." He then left MIT in 2010 to join Stripe, and says dropping out twice "is something that I do not wish on anyone’s parents."
claims.inference: Repeated moves toward stronger peers and away from a role (club leader) where he felt he could not yet perform at the level the role implied.
claims.alternative: Could reflect a learning drive (Type 5) or a desire for belonging among the best (Type 6/2). The parents line shows the choice had a cost.

claims.claim: At Stripe he built systems in sprints "working from wake until sleep" and wrote in 2017: "These are the times I feel most alive"; he cites the credit-card vault built in his two weeks home for the 2010 holidays, an authorization flow in three weeks instead of 6–12 months, a 24-hour sprint to get onto the card networks, and a rule of "soft" and "hard" launch dates ("I’ve never hit a soft launch date, but have never missed a hard one").
claims.inference: Aliveness located in high-output delivery against deadlines; speed and shipping over process.
claims.alternative: Startup norms reward exactly this; many engineers of different types describe flow this way. Fortune independently reports he often coded through the night.

claims.claim: By 2013–14, stacking every engineer’s 1:1 on Tuesdays left him "completely burned out by the end of the day"; his first-ever vacation came only after hiring a VP Engineering, and he chose to return to coding on the principle that "it’s not about time management, it’s about energy management," ending: "I’m too busy coding."
claims.inference: He chooses the activity where he is most effective and energized over the people-management role; the "first ever" vacation at about 26 fits a pattern repeated in 2024.
claims.alternative: Energy conservation and meeting fatigue ("a single meeting will kill productivity," S04) are also classic Type 5 markers. Introversion, not type, may explain them.

claims.claim: In 2014 he admitted "having trouble distinguishing “not the way I’d do it” from “bad”" when a new executive ran things differently, and called "sparse micromanagement"—"jumping in to some random issue, overturning all the decisions, and then disappearing"—"the worst."
claims.inference: Candid self-criticism about judging others’ methods; the principle is notable because later colleagues describe him jumping into others’ projects and working around people (C33, C31).
claims.alternative: The judging habit is a Type 1 marker (the strongest alternative). The irony with later reports is interpretation; the later reports are anonymous and contested.

claims.claim: Across twelve years he describes caring about shaping the environment around the work: in 2014, "I had a very strong vision of the environment I wanted to be a part of, and I was willing to go out of my way to make it exist"; in 2026 he says he will trade "type one fun" for "type two fun" to build an environment where others do great work, and that his career has been about "really helping to build and shape environments and culture."
claims.inference: Stable self-concept as culture builder; complicates a pure individual-achiever reading.
claims.alternative: Supports a 3w2 shading or a 2/6 alternative; also standard founder self-description.

claims.claim: He left Stripe in May 2015, as its CTO and fourth employee, having "successfully removed myself as a critical lynchpin," because he was "yearning to create something of my own," had "topped out the S-curve" of learning, and feared he would "always wonder what could have been." In 2016 he added that developer infrastructure "wasn’t the problem that I wanted to work on for the rest of my life," and in 2026 that Stripe’s problem "was not my problem."
claims.inference: A costly exit from a secure, prestigious role toward something "of my own" and bigger. Fits an achievement/significance drive; argues against a Type 2 need to be needed (he celebrated being unneeded).
claims.alternative: Also fits Type 7 (topped-out novelty) or simple ambition. The 2026 "not my problem" framing is retrospective.

claims.claim: After a July 2015 dinner, he "volunteered myself as tribute" to go full time on the unformed lab, recruited the founding team, hosted the first office in his apartment, fetched the whiteboard the researchers lacked, and "resolved to do whatever was needed to remove all non-research tasks from Ilya’s plate."
claims.inference: Willingness to take any role in service of the project; shows role flexibility toward a goal.
claims.alternative: Self-effacing service also fits Type 2 or 9. The same posts present him as the indispensable organizer, so humility and centrality coexist.

claims.claim: In January 2017 he wrote that he found his role "not by seeking it — instead, I sought out a problem more important to me than my role within it," and that although coding is "the activity I love most in the world... people remain my focus."
claims.inference: His stated hierarchy: mission over role, people over code.
claims.alternative: Public self-presentation written as a recruiting post; it can be read as a 9-like self-forgetting or a 3’s identification with the goal.

claims.claim: He repeatedly describes others’ response to his work as what makes it matter: "the deep satisfaction of having others actually use my creations" (2015); "something extremely validating about your work allowing researchers to ask questions" (2017); "the team’s excitement every time I overcame a new obstacle was deeply validating" (2019); "the most glorious feeling" when 1,500 people played his game (2026).
claims.inference: A recurring, spontaneous vocabulary of validation tied to accomplishment registered by others: a core Type 3 marker when combined with C17.
claims.alternative: A Type 2 would also prize others’ appreciation; a healthy builder of any type enjoys users. Weight comes from the recurrence across 11 years, not any single line.

claims.claim: His own account of learning machine learning: for three years he "procrastinat[ed]" while his software skills were in demand; on Dota, when colleagues treated his work as impressive, "I always made sure to correct them by pointing out that I was a newbie"; when a colleague got better results without his code, "I had nothing to show for my efforts. I never tried machine learning on the Dota project again." He returned in private holiday self-study in late 2018, sustained by a new relationship with "someone who made me feel it was ok if I failed," and concluded he had been "unwilling to become a beginner again."
claims.inference: The clearest discriminating evidence: a sustained block organized around visible competence ("nothing to show," managing others’ estimate of him) and resolved only where failure was safe and unobserved. This is the Type 3 fear of failing in view, more than a Type 1 fear of doing it wrong or a Type 5 retreat to master knowledge for its own sake (he says "I learn best when I have something specific in mind to build").
claims.alternative: Type 5 (fear of incompetence) and Type 6 (needing safety to risk) both partly explain it. The essay is also shaped as an inspirational lesson for recruits.

claims.claim: In 2022 he named the key trait for engineers moving into ML as "a specific flavor of technical humility": being "happy to be wrong" and not "afraid not to know something."
claims.inference: The lesson he drew from his own block (C17), suggesting the image cost of not-knowing was real to him.
claims.alternative: Generic advice; weak alone.

claims.claim: He has described the mission in consistent terms for a decade: 2019, "making AGI go well is the most important problem I can imagine contributing towards"; 2019 to Lex Fridman, building it means "you stop thinking about yourself so much"; April 2026, "people don’t understand how focused I am on this mission in a way that I think has been very personally painful at many turns," and success is "Achieving the open AI mission"; May 2026 under oath, "Solving for the mission has always been my primary motivation... It remains so today."
claims.inference: Total identification with the mission. For the Type 3 reading, the mission is the goal his worth is fused with; for Type 1, it is a moral cause.
claims.alternative: Strong incentives: recruiting, PR and, at trial, a legal defense against greed claims. Consistency over time is real, but self-report cannot establish motive.

claims.claim: Karen Hao, embedded at OpenAI in 2019, found him "nervous and guarded" ("We’ve never given someone so much access before"); he "recites the charter like scripture," then volunteered that he knew the lines because he had pored over them "to get them exactly right. It’s not like I was reading this before the meeting." He drew heavily on heroic stories (the moon-shot janitor, the transcontinental railroad, Edison).
claims.inference: Close attention to how he comes across (pre-empting the impression of reading a script) alongside exacting precision about the mission text.
claims.alternative: The precision and scripture-like devotion are the strongest single support for the Type 1 alternative; nervousness with a reporter is situational.

claims.claim: He married Anna in November 2019 at OpenAI’s offices on a workday, after about a year of dating; Ilya Sutskever officiated and a robotic hand served as ring bearer.
claims.inference: Work and personal life fused; a vivid detail of identification with the company.
claims.alternative: A deliberate, joyful choice, possibly Anna’s too; do not psychologize beyond the facts.

claims.claim: Brockman’s private 2017 diary, produced in the Musk litigation, includes "Happy to not become rich on this, so long as no one else is"; the question "So what do I *really* want?" with an answer including "Financially what will take me to $1B"; "cannot say that we are committed to the non-profit . . . if three months later we’re doing b-corp then it was a lie"; and, in November 2017, that converting to a b-corp without Musk would be "pretty morally bankrupt."
claims.inference: Contemporaneous private evidence of conflicting instincts: wealth as a personal target, fairness/relative-wealth language, and a moral and reputational check on how the for-profit move would look.
claims.alternative: Outlets render the wording differently ("Financially, what will take me to $1B?" in S27; a longer November entry with "he’s really not an idiot" in S25). Quote one outlet’s version with attribution. Musk’s lawyers chose the excerpts; Brockman says the writings were for himself.

claims.claim: Testifying on May 4–5, 2026, Brockman was "serene, even chipper" recalling early days but "grew agitated" under cross-examination; he said "Solving for the mission has always been my primary motivation," explained the diary line as "I meant it would actually serve the mission, but it’d be hard to look at yourself in the mirror," and, asked why he had not donated his roughly $29 billion stake, said "I don’t think about it like that," calling the for-profit "built through blood, sweat and tears."
claims.inference: His own gloss locates the 2017 obstacle in how the act would reflect on him ("look at yourself in the mirror") while conceding it would have served the goal. That fits an image-and-effectiveness frame better than a pure rule frame.
claims.alternative: A Type 1 also uses "mirror" language for conscience. Trial testimony is adversarial and lawyered.

claims.claim: He disclosed in court that his OpenAI stake is worth nearly $30 billion though he invested no money, and conceded that a $100,000 personal donation he had discussed with early nonprofit donors such as Musk, Reid Hoffman and Marissa Mayer was never made; Forbes named him the richest newcomer on the 2026 Forbes 400, at an estimated $25.5 billion as of September 4, 2026.
claims.inference: Establishes the scale of the wealth question in C22 and C41.
claims.alternative: Courthouse News’s wording on the $100,000 is ambiguous about whether it was a pledge; one secondary summary calls it an unpaid pledge (not used). Figures differ (Forbes says he swore to "more than $20 billion"); valuations move. Date any figure.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check net worth and stake value at any OpenAI IPO filing, tender offer or the next Forbes/Bloomberg update; always print the as-of date.

claims.claim: In September 2017 Sutskever sent Musk and Altman an email signed "Greg & Ilya" admitting they had withheld concerns because "we were afraid of harming the relationship, having you think less of us, or losing you as partners," that they were "much worse at being a counterbalance" to Musk than Altman, that they had "allowed the idea of financial return 2-3 years down the line to drive our decisions," and "did not speak our full truth." Two days later they told Zilis they would continue as a nonprofit.
claims.inference: Jointly authored evidence of reluctance to confront a powerful partner and concern with how they were seen, then a costly confession.
claims.alternative: Cannot be assigned to Brockman alone. The fear of "harming the relationship" fits Types 9/6/2 as well as 3. Use cautiously and attribute to both.

claims.claim: His own early emails to Musk show deference and ambition together: in November 2015 he did not want to "pull any punches" and hoped to "shift the dialog towards being about humanity winning rather than any particular group or company"; in February 2016, "I don't yet feel comfortable making decisions here on my own, and would love any guidance," answering Musk’s "whatever it takes" with "Read you loud and clear. Sounds like a plan."
claims.inference: A capable operator seeking the principal’s approval on high-stakes calls early in a new role.
claims.alternative: Guidance-seeking is a Type 6 marker; it is also ordinary for a 28-year-old running a donor-funded lab. Weak alone.

claims.claim: He testified that in August 2017 Musk demanded majority equity, board control and the CEO title, that when Brockman and Sutskever proposed equal shares Musk said "I decline" and "stormed around the table"—"I actually thought he was going to hit me"—and that "The one thing we could not accept was to hand him unilateral, absolute control, potentially, over the AGI." His July 2017 email had laid out a path from nonprofit to "AI research + hardware for-profit (starting 2018)."
claims.inference: He backed a for-profit path early while resisting one person’s control; useful context for C22.
claims.alternative: Adversarial testimony in his own defense; Musk disputes the account. Not personality evidence on its own.

claims.claim: Several accounts say Brockman floated raising money by selling AGI access to governments around 2017–18: policy adviser Page Hedley recalls "Greg kept going back to ‘So how do we raise more money? How do we win?’", Jack Clark described a "prisoner’s dilemma" for nations, and the WSJ reports he named the UN Security Council’s nuclear powers. Brockman maintains he "never seriously entertained" auctioning models; an OpenAI representative called the characterization "utterly ridiculous."
claims.inference: If accurate, a strong ends-over-means and winning orientation in fundraising, consistent with C33.
claims.alternative: Contested, from people in the rival Amodei camp and a policy adviser; Brockman denies it. It cannot carry the type argument. Present both sides.
claims.review_trigger: Update if Brockman, Hedley or Clark give new on-record accounts or if court exhibits on the "countries plan" become public.

claims.claim: Dario Amodei’s private notes record that, pressed on his priorities, Brockman said he wanted "money and power"; Brockman disputes this.
claims.inference: If true, a candid wealth-and-status motive consistent with the $1B diary line.
claims.alternative: A rival’s private recollection, released without Brockman’s context; he denies it. Sensitive. Do not present as fact; it should not be load-bearing.
claims.review_trigger: Update only if a second contemporaneous source or Brockman’s own account surfaces.

claims.claim: After Musk left in 2018, according to the WSJ, employees lacked faith in Brockman and Sutskever’s leadership after layoffs; Dario Amodei stayed on condition that they not be in charge, and the New Yorker reports that "some considered" Brockman "an abrasive operator" and that Altman assured researchers his managerial authority would be diminished.
claims.inference: Independent outlets converge on friction over his management by 2018.
claims.alternative: Sources are largely unnamed and include the Amodeis’ allies. The layoffs were requested by Musk (S22). Present as reported friction, not a finding.

claims.claim: The WSJ reports that in 2018–19 Brockman sought a role on the language-model project; Daniela Amodei, its co-lead, offered to step down rather than allow it, Alec Radford reportedly did not want to work with him, and "Brockman and Altman reluctantly agreed to keep Brockman off the language project."
claims.inference: He pushed to be where the frontier work was and appealed over a peer’s head; others resisted his involvement.
claims.alternative: Unnamed sourcing; Radford reportedly felt used in a proxy war. Brockman’s side is not given.

claims.claim: In March 2020, asked by Altman to write peer reviews, Brockman wrote "a lengthy piece of feedback" accusing Daniela Amodei of "abusing her power to create bureaucratic processes to get her way"; Altman called it "tough but fair," she rebutted it point by point, and Brockman at one point offered to withdraw it.
claims.inference: He attacked process as an obstacle (anti-bureaucracy), engaged conflict directly, then offered to retract when it escalated. Useful for the 1-versus-3 discriminator: he opposed procedure rather than defending it.
claims.alternative: The fairness charge ("abusing her power") is also Type 1 moral language. Unnamed sourcing; Daniela disputes his critique.

claims.claim: Colleagues describe extreme pace and impatience: he once set Slack to notify him of every message company-wide; a former engineer chose carefully whom to assign to him "because you weren’t going to be sleeping"; "He’d go super hard, then go off like a bear and hibernate for a few weeks"; "He has incredibly high standards and expects results"; "If something’s not moving fast enough, Greg will take it into his own hands and work around people if necessary... He’s very much an ends-over-means kind of person." AMD CEO Lisa Su praised his "maniacal focus" and recalled his stance as "Failure is not an option."
claims.inference: Third-party convergence on results-first intensity and boom-bust work cycles. "Ends-over-means" directly discriminates against Type 1.
claims.alternative: Most quotes are anonymous; Su is a deal partner. Hard-driving pace also fits Types 8 and 7. Use as reported description with attribution.

claims.claim: Before the November 2023 ouster, Sutskever sent the board a memo critical of Brockman, as he confirmed under oath in October 2025; Fortune, citing Keach Hagey’s book, reports it concerned "alleged bullying." OpenAI says "These claims aren’t true," noting Sutskever signed the petition for Brockman’s return. In the same deposition Sutskever said his note that Brockman was "essentially fired from Stripe" came only from Mira Murati and that he never verified it.
claims.inference: Documents that serious internal complaints existed; their content is not public.
claims.alternative: Sensitive and unproven. The memo’s text is not public; the Hagey/Murati details (S09) come from an unopened book. The Stripe-firing hearsay is contradicted by his own account and contemporaneous reporting and should not appear except, if at all, as an unverified claim Sutskever admitted he never checked.
claims.review_trigger: Update if the Brockman memo is released, Hagey’s or Hao’s book passages are opened, or Murati/Sutskever speak on record.

claims.claim: On November 17, 2023, Sutskever told him on a Google Meet that he was removed from the board but "vital to the company" and would keep his role; within hours he posted the note he sent staff: "but based on today’s news, i quit... i continue to believe in the mission of creating safe AGI that benefits all of humanity." He recalls thinking "It just wasn't right"; asked if it was anger, "No. I felt like I understood what had happened"; he told his wife "Got to quit," and she said "I agree."
claims.inference: His most consequential costly choice: giving up position and equity security in hours, in solidarity with Altman. Loyalty and a moral verdict ("wasn’t right"), with anger denied.
claims.alternative: Denying anger while judging something "not right" is a classic Type 1 pattern (also 9). Loyalty to the winning partner also fits pragmatic 3; he estimated a 10% chance of getting the company back and began planning a new company with Altman the same day.

claims.claim: Asked in 2026 about the loyalty he inspired in November 2023, he became emotional: "I'm very much a in the trenches kind of leader. Try to lead from the front. And sometimes when I do that, I don't always Sorry, I'm getting a little emotional. Um, but I don't always look back to see if everyone's following. Like I just run right in." He said no one accepted a competing offer that weekend.
claims.inference: Self-image as the leader who charges ahead; strong feeling at being followed and validated by his people.
claims.alternative: Lead-from-the-front language fits Type 8; the emotion about loyalty fits 2 and 6. A live audio moment, but in a friendly, edited interview.

claims.claim: He returned with Altman on November 21–22, 2023; after the WilmerHale review the board said on March 8, 2024 that it had "full confidence" in both men.
claims.inference: Outcome of the crisis; official vindication.
claims.alternative: The review was not published; the statement is the company’s.

claims.claim: He calls Sutskever’s departure "maybe the only moment in OpenAI's history where I felt like I didn't want to do it anymore." In August 2024 he announced a sabbatical—"First time to relax since co-founding OpenAI 9 years ago"—during which he trained DNA language models for the Arc Institute, a field meaningful to him and his wife, who "has a lot of health conditions"; he returned in November: "longest vacation of my life complete. back to building."
claims.inference: Nine years without a break, a collapse of motivation when a key partner left, then rest that was itself more building. Matches the "bear" cycle in C33.
claims.alternative: Fortune reports outlets tied the sabbatical to concerns about his leadership style; OpenAI says it was his decision (S19). Both may be true.

claims.claim: He frames his recent growth as overcoming indecision and conflict-avoidance: he has approached OpenAI "through a lens of uncertainty," trying to reconcile everyone’s strong opinions; he has worked to "have a stronger sense of self"; his regrets are when "we just waited too long"; and his lesson learned more than once is "Make the hard decision. Have the hard conversation." He told Stratechery that 2023 showed "interpersonal tensions... that we had not sufficiently gotten ahead of."
claims.inference: The strongest material for a Type 9 (or 6) reading: merging opinions, weak sense of self, avoided hard conversations.
claims.alternative: Leadership-lesson clichés suited to the podcast format and post-2023 narrative; they sit oddly with third-party accounts of him writing a harsh critique and working around people (C32, C33).

claims.claim: After returning he led a new Scaling group and OpenAI’s infrastructure build-out, including Stargate and chip deals; a direct report calls him "some of the secret sauce" behind the deals, and Forbes says that since July 2026 he also oversees OpenAI’s product business, making him second-in-command. A Washington consultant told Fortune he "is not super-independent from Sam."
claims.inference: Executor of Altman’s vision with growing scope.
claims.alternative: Titles and scope change; the "not independent" view is a single anonymous outsider.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check title, reporting line and scope at drafting and on any OpenAI leadership announcement or IPO filing.

claims.claim: He and his wife gave $25 million to the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc. in 2025 and pledged $50 million to Leading the Future, a pro-AI super PAC he helped launch, while OpenAI’s official stance is that the company will not contribute to such PACs; OpenAI said his involvement was "in a personal capacity." In June 2026, according to The New York Times, he told colleagues on Slack "I feel terrible about the fact that LTF keeps reflecting on the company and become so much of a distraction for people here," that they had given $25 million and had "no plans to donate more at this time."
claims.inference: A bold, costly public bet followed by a reversal justified by the reputational cost to the company and colleagues, not by calling the giving wrong. Fits the effectiveness/image frame of the discriminator.
claims.alternative: Inner motive for the donations is unknown; WIRED’s interview (S21, unopened) gives his own rationale. The New Yorker’s "this year" wording on the MAGA gift conflicts with 2025 dating elsewhere; date it as reported in 2025. Political material is sensitive; keep it factual.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check after the Nov. 3, 2026 midterms and any FEC filings or new statements from Brockman about either PAC; open the NYT report and the WIRED interview before quoting.

claims.claim: In 2016 he wrote that Altman’s answer "To build safe human-level AI" convinced him because "sometimes an effort needs only someone bold enough to pronounce a goal, and then the right people will join them." Ten years later he closed the GPT-6 Astra briefing on September 3, 2026 with "Welcome to the AGI era," saying of AGI "I think it might be about this model"; in his pre-launch Stratechery interview he hedged: "maybe it was the previous model, maybe it’s Astra, maybe it’s the next model."
claims.inference: A durable belief in the power of bold public pronouncement, which he now enacts as OpenAI’s launch spokesman.
claims.alternative: Launch-day statements are marketing; the claim is contested by critics. Keep the dated quotes; avoid treating the AGI claim as settled.
claims.review_trigger: Update if OpenAI or Brockman formally declares or retracts an AGI determination, or if the Astra claim is materially revised.

claims.claim: In early 2016 he argued at the Amodei group house that AI’s makers needed to inform "all 300 million Americans about what was coming," while Dario Amodei and Holden Karnofsky favored telling the government first; he says he was probably the one who named OpenAI’s "iterative deployment" approach.
claims.inference: Long-standing preference for public release and broadcast over quiet caution.
claims.alternative: The WSJ notes this is Brockman’s takeaway from the exchange; also a business-strategy disagreement, not just temperament.

claims.claim: He says that at OpenAI, "the question of who gets credit for a particular thing... suddenly takes on this existential weight," and agrees that wanting to be "front and center" is "the overwhelming dynamic that I have observed in this field"; the WSJ reports Dario Amodei resented Brockman discussing the charter on a podcast and being left out of an Obama meeting Brockman attended with Altman.
claims.inference: Credit and visibility were live issues around him; he names them in others.
claims.alternative: He attributes the dynamic to the field, not himself; the WSJ episodes reflect Amodei’s grievances, not Brockman’s motives.

claims.claim: He says moving from hands-on coding to leading "has been something for me that was difficult, because you had to let go of something that I was used to and valued and really loved. But I’ve actually replaced it with something I love even more," and, asked if he will ever have a 24-hour coding session again: "I hope so... but I will say that I have found so much joy and value in helping the team in the way that I do now."
claims.inference: Shift of identity from maker to leader; joy relocated to the team’s output.
claims.alternative: Also consistent with Type 2 shading; it is a 2026 reflection during a launch promotion.

claims.claim: He repeatedly says the work is about people: "I cared most about working with great people to make something amazing happen" (2016); "for me, it’s always been about the people" and "it’s always about the people, in good and bad ways" (2026).
claims.inference: Relational emphasis that a pure achiever reading must account for (wing or alternative).
claims.alternative: Common founder rhetoric; supports 2/6/9 alternatives or a 3w2.

claims.claim: Under Ben Thompson’s pressing about OpenAI’s security lapse before the July 2026 Hugging Face breach, he conceded "there’s time that defenders lost" while reframing that "time is not all made equally" and that acting earlier would have produced "much less progress."
claims.inference: Defends the team’s record while partly conceding: image-of-competence management under critique.
claims.alternative: Ordinary corporate communications posture; executives of any type do this. Low weight.
claims.review_trigger: Update if investigations or OpenAI disclosures change the Hugging Face incident account.

claims.claim: Guadagnino’s film Artificial, in which Cooper Hoffman plays Brockman (listed as OpenAI’s board chairman), premiered at the New York Film Festival on October 5, 2026, with a U.S. release by Neon set for December 25, 2026.
claims.inference: Explains current search interest; not personality evidence.
claims.alternative: Release plans can change; the film is a dramatization, not a source.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check after the Dec. 25, 2026 release for reviews of the Brockman portrayal and any Brockman or OpenAI response.

claims.claim: In January 2018 he told Musk that "Ilya and I are able to convince reputable people that AGI can really happen in the next ≤10 years" and proposed building custom AI hardware and a "Massive AI data center" within three years, the compute thesis he later executed through Stargate.
claims.inference: Long-horizon consistency of his strategic bet on compute; context for "builder-in-chief."
claims.alternative: Business strategy, not motive.

claims.claim: In his 2016 account of the founding dinner he says he admired Musk as inquisitive and someone who "sought others opinions and really listened," and that Sutskever was "a source of grounding."
claims.inference: Minor; shows admiration for partners he would later testify against (Musk).
claims.alternative: Diplomatic writing about a then-funder.

claims.claim: Interpretation for the thesis: across 2014–2026 his costliest choices cluster around staying at the point of visible, high-output building and around how his competence and commitment register with others—choosing the field where he could be "best in the world," leaving roles once he was no longer the engine, abandoning ML when he had "nothing to show," working nine years without rest then crashing, and reversing a public political bet when it cost the company’s standing.
claims.inference: This is the Type 3 argument in compressed form; each link must be shown with the dated evidence above.
claims.alternative: A Type 1 reading reorganizes the same choices around doing the right thing well (see type_hypothesis.alternative_case). Mission identification and startup incentives explain some of the intensity regardless of type.

claims.claim: Interpretation for the alternative: his moral vocabulary recurs—"pretty morally bankrupt" (2017 diary), "It just wasn't right" with anger denied (2023), the charter learned "exactly right" and recited "like scripture" (2019), his self-confessed habit of treating "not the way I’d do it" as "bad" (2014), and "encounter the hard truth" (2026)—which is the strongest case for Type 1.
claims.inference: Must be presented near the main type argument as the strongest alternative.
claims.alternative: Each item has a non-1 reading: the mirror gloss (C23) frames morality as self-image; ends-over-means and anti-bureaucracy (C32, C33) cut against 1.

type_hypothesis.against: Real evidence resists Type 3. (1) Moral vocabulary recurs across a decade: "pretty morally bankrupt" in the 2017 diary (C22), "It just wasn't right" with anger explicitly denied on the day he quit (C35), learning the charter "exactly right" and reciting it "like scripture" (C20), his 2014 admission that he treats "not the way I’d do it" as "bad" (C11), the "abusing her power" charge in his 2020 peer review (C32), and "incredibly high standards" (C33). That is the Type 1 case (C52). (2) He repeatedly steps out of status roles: choosing to code rather than manage at Stripe (C10), celebrating that he was no longer a "lynchpin" (C13), fetching whiteboards and taking non-research work off Sutskever’s plate (C14), and saying people, not his role, are his focus (C15, C46). A classic image-driven 3 would be expected to hold the visible executive seat. (3) His 2026 self-account stresses indecision, a weak "sense of self," avoided "hard conversations" and synthesizing others’ opinions (C39), and the jointly signed 2017 email admits withholding concerns for fear of "harming the relationship" (C25); his early emails ask Musk for "guidance" (C26). That supports Type 9 or 6. (4) His loyalty on November 17, 2023 cost him position immediately and he wept over the loyalty others showed him (C35, C36), which fits 2/6 as well as 3. (5) Incentives explain much: startup and lab cultures reward all-night sprints; mission talk is recruiting, PR and, in May 2026, a legal defense against greed claims (C19, C23). (6) Much of the friction evidence is anonymous or comes from his rivals, the Amodeis (C28–C34), and some is disputed outright.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 1 is the strongest rival. It explains the moral and correctness language above, the devotion to a written charter he worked to get "exactly right" (C20), a reformer’s conviction that the mission is the most important problem (C19), the judging habit he admits (C11), fairness language ("Happy to not become rich on this, so long as no one else is," C22; "abusing her power," C32), high standards and impatience (C33), the moral verdict and denied anger on November 17 (C35), and the self-control of working nine years without rest (C38). Type 9 is a credible third: role-flexible self-effacement (C14, C15), his 2026 account of uncertainty, a weak sense of self and avoided hard conversations (C39), the fear of harming relationships in the 2017 email (C25), and a pattern of executing Altman’s vision (C40). It fails to explain his pushing into others’ projects, a harsh written critique, working around people, and his performer’s history (C31–C33, C04–C05). Type 6 (loyalty, guidance-seeking, team belonging, C26, C35, C46) is weaker because he shows little threat-scanning or doubt about authority and is publicly optimistic. Type 5 is undercut because he treats knowledge as instrumental ("I learn best when I have something specific in mind to build," C17) and leads publicly. Type 8 is undercut by his self-reported reluctance to confront Musk and to have hard conversations (C25, C39). Type 2 is undercut by his celebrating being unneeded and leaving (C13). Wing and subtype are optional. A 3w2 or self-preservation 3 would account for the work-ethic, people-focus and low-flash style, but should not be used to explain away the Type 1 evidence.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: When doing it the right way and winning or looking competent conflict, which does he protect, and how does he justify his own reversals? A Type 1 should hold process and principle at a cost to speed and should frame reversals as correcting a wrong. Brockman’s record leans the other way: he prizes shipping speed (soft vs hard launch dates, overnight integrations, an API hacked together over a holiday weekend; C09, C33), is described by a former colleague as "ends-over-means" and willing to "work around people" (C33), attacked a colleague’s process as "bureaucratic" rather than defending procedure (C32), explained his 2017 "morally bankrupt" diary entry under oath as "it would actually serve the mission, but it’d be hard to look at yourself in the mirror" (C23), and reversed his $50 million PAC pledge because it was "reflecting on the company" and becoming a "distraction," not because the giving was wrong (C41). His one documented competence crisis was organized around visible results and others’ estimate of him ("nothing to show," correcting people who rated him highly) and resolved only where failure was "ok" and unobserved (C17), which is the 3 fear of failing in view rather than the 1 fear of being wrong. Limits: several discriminating items are anonymous (C33), reported by rivals (C32), relayed through a second outlet (C41), or are testimony with legal incentives (C23). The discriminator rests on the convergence of self-report (C17, C23) with third-party description, not on any single item.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The moral vocabulary itself (C22, C35, C52) is not fully dissolved by the 3 reading; neither is the depth of his emotion about followers’ loyalty (C36) or the repeated willingness to drop status roles and do grunt work (C10, C13, C14). The jointly written 2017 confession of fearing to confront Musk (C25) and his own 2026 account of indecision (C39) fit 9 better than 3. The "Happy to not become rich... so long as no one else is" line (C22) mixes fairness and comparison and has no single reading. The inner motive for his 2025 political donations is unknown (C41; the WIRED interview, S21, was not opened). The content of the Sutskever memo (C34) and the truth of the "money and power" and "countries plan" accounts (C28, C29) are unresolved.
